reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: A slow-growing photochromogen (producing yellow pigment on exposure to light) that is one of the more virulent nontuberculous mycobacteria
Acquired chiefly from municipal tap water rather than soil, with geographical clustering in certain regions and among miners and industrial workers
Produces the most tuberculosis-like illness of the nontuberculous mycobacteria, with chronic cavitary upper-lobe pulmonary disease, cough, and haemoptysis
Most often affects middle-aged men with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pneumoconiosis, or previous tuberculosis
Isolation is rarely due to simple contamination, so a positive respiratory culture usually reflects genuine disease
Carries the ESAT-6 and CFP-10 antigens and can therefore cause a positive interferon-gamma release assay, adding to the confusion with tuberculosis
Rifampicin is the cornerstone of therapy, combined with agents such as ethambutol and a macrolide or isoniazid, and rifampicin susceptibility should be tested
Responds well to rifampicin-based combination treatment, giving one of the better outcomes among the nontuberculous mycobacteria
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium kansasii is a slow-growing photochromogenic mycobacterium whose principal reservoir is treated water-distribution systems. Inhalation leads to pulmonary infection in hosts with pre-existing lung damage, where it produces a granulomatous, frequently cavitating process closely resembling tuberculosis. Impaired cell-mediated immunity, notably advanced HIV infection, predisposes to disseminated disease and extrapulmonary sites such as lymph nodes, skin, and joints. Because the organism expresses antigens shared with M. tuberculosis, immune-based tests can cross-react. Its comparatively predictable susceptibility to rifampicin underlies the good response to rifampicin-based regimens.
additionalDifferentials: Other cavitary NTM lung disease (M. xenopi, M. malmoense)
additionalInvestigations: Mycobacterial culture with recognition of photochromogenic pigment
Molecular identification to distinguish it from M. tuberculosis and other NTM
Rifampicin susceptibility testing of the isolate
Chest radiograph and CT for upper-lobe cavitary or fibronodular disease
Repeated sputum cultures to meet diagnostic criteria
HIV testing and immune assessment, especially with disseminated disease
redFlags: Disseminated disease indicating advanced immunosuppression such as HIV
Diagnostic confusion leading to treatment for tuberculosis and delay in correct therapy
reference.prognosis: With rifampicin-based combination therapy the prognosis is generally favourable and relapse is uncommon in adherent patients, making M. kansasii one of the more treatable nontuberculous mycobacteria. Rifampicin resistance, extensive structural lung damage, and significant immunosuppression worsen outcomes.
pitfalls: Mistaking the illness and a positive interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis
Dismissing a positive culture as a contaminant when it usually signifies real disease
Under-treating with an inadequate or single-drug regimen
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ATS/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial diseases
management: Treat with a prolonged rifampicin-based combination regimen, typically rifampicin, ethambutol, and either isoniazid or a macrolide, which achieves reliably good outcomes
Perform rifampicin susceptibility testing to confirm the isolate remains rifampicin-susceptible and guide the regimen
Manage the underlying structural lung disease, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, alongside antimycobacterial treatment
Monitor for drug toxicity, including ethambutol-related ocular toxicity with visual monitoring and hepatotoxicity, and track response with repeated sputum cultures
Perform HIV testing and immune assessment, treating disseminated disease more intensively and starting antiretroviral therapy where indicated while accounting for rifamycin interactions
Refer to infectious diseases or respiratory medicine, noting the generally favourable prognosis and low relapse rate in adherent patients
